tier_reason: The paper (arXiv 2304.11012 v3, ESA 2023) compares LeMonHash with the named MMPHF baselines: Hollow Trie, Centroid Hollow Trie, Path Decomposed Trie, ZFast, PaCo and LCP variants. Section 8 states the Intel Xeon E5-2670 v3 CPU, GNU C++ 11.1.0 and -O3 -march=native. The benchmark code is public in ByteHamster/MMPHF-Experiments (cpp/comparison.cpp with cpp/benchmark/*Contender.h, java/src/main/java/com/bytehamster/mmphfexperiments/Main.java, scripts/runExperiments.sh). That meets every Tier A condition.

corrections.baseline: Prior monotone MPHF implementations: the Grossi-Ottaviano C++ Centroid Hollow Trie, Hollow Trie and Path Decomposed Trie (ot/path_decomposed_tries), plus the Belazzougui et al. Java implementations from Sux4J of the Hollow Trie Distributor, Hollow Trie, ZFast Trie, LCP, LCP 2-step, PaCo, VLLCP and VLPaCo
corrections.claimed_speedup: Abstract: on synthetic random integers, 34% less space than the next larger competitor with about 16x faster queries; on real-world data, up to 19x faster queries than the next larger competitor at similar or better space; up to 2x faster construction than the competitor with the next best space usage (typically Hollow Trie variants); LeMonHash-VL (strings) is within 13% of the best competitors' space with up to 3x faster queries than the next larger competitor. Derived from page data (Table A.1): on uniform keys, 2718 vs 179 kQueries/s = 15.2x against the Java (Sux4J) Hollow Trie at 2.98 vs 4.54 bits/key; against the C++ Hollow Trie (351 kq/s, 4.61 bpk) it is 7.7x; on osm, 1338 vs 73 kq/s = 18.3x against the Java HTDist.
corrections.caveats: The headline 16x and 19x ratios are against Java (Sux4J) implementations, run on OpenJDK 17 with one unmeasured JIT warm-up run. Against the fastest C++ competitor at similar space, the gap is about 7-8x (derived from Table A.1). The comparison covers only academic MMPHF implementations, not BBHash, CMPH, PTHash, std::map or a sorted-array binary search. An MMPHF preserves key order (it returns the key's rank), so it is a different problem from a plain MPHF. The integer variant supports integer keys only; LeMonHash-VL covers strings. The Path Decomposed Trie crashes on integer inputs. Each experiment ran only twice and was averaged (the paper says variation is small).

notes: All numbers in claimed_speedup appear in the abstract, and Table A.1 supports them: 15.2x uniform, 15.7x normal, 13.3x exponential, 18.3x osm, all against the next-larger-space competitor. The baseline field's claim about replacing std::map or binary search was not on the page, so I removed it. License GPL-3.0, 32 stars, last commit 2026-09-13 and not a fork all match gh.

reject_reason: other: MQF is a counting quotient filter, not an MPHF, and its only comparison against a listed baseline (BBHash, Fig. S6) is invalid because the published harness never performs the MQF lookup
tier_reason: The paper (BMC Bioinformatics 22:71) says MQF block labels are ~10x faster than BBHash; Supplementary Fig. S6 shows about 300 ms for MQF vs about 3,100-3,550 ms for BBHash over 35M queries. The only harness for that figure is taggingTest.cpp in dib-lab/2020-paper-mqf-benchmarks (the same file is on the MQF 'benchmark' branch). It builds the MQF through Benchmark_Utils_Script/countingStructure.hpp with qf_init(..., blocksLabelSize=0, ...), so itemOrder() in gqf.cpp returns 0 immediately at `if(qf->metadata->BlockLabel_bits!=32) return 0;` and never searches the filter. That leaves no valid numbers against the baseline.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Paper claims ~10x faster queries than BBHash for 35M existing k-mers, with MQF query time flat across 60-90% load (Fig. S6 bars, read from the chart: MQF about 300 ms, i.e. about 8.6 ns/query, vs BBHash about 3,100-3,550 ms, i.e. about 89-101 ns/query; derived from page data). The published benchmark code makes the MQF side a no-op, so this result is not supported.
corrections.workload: 35M existing k-mers (k=25) queried against MQFs of 255 MB loaded to 60/70/80/90%, each MQF paired with a BBHash MPHF (rizkg/BBHash, default options, 1 thread) of 15-22 MB built on the same k-mer set. MQF 'labels' means the item's order in the filter, computed by itemOrder().
corrections.caveats: MQF is a counting quotient filter that stores the keys. Its block labels act like an MPHF only for stored keys, and the MQF used 255 MB where BBHash used 15-22 MB (about 12-17x more memory, derived). In the published harness (taggingTest.cpp plus countingStructure.hpp), the MQF is created with block-label size 0, so qf_ComputeItemsOrder() and itemOrder() return early. The timed MQF loop therefore measures only ihash() and a call that returns 0. The Fig. S6 figures of about 8.6 ns/query on a 255 MB structure fit a no-op. CPU model (AWS t3.large, burstable) and compiler version are not stated. BBHash is also no longer the fastest MPHF baseline.

notes: Category check as requested: MQF is not an MPHF. Its only comparison against a listed baseline for this category is BBHash in Fig. S6, and the published code for that figure never runs the MQF lookup (blocksLabelSize=0 in every version of countingStructure.hpp I checked, back to 2019). I cannot rule out an unpublished local change, but the paper says all experiment code is in that repo. Metadata matches gh: BSD-3-Clause, 12 stars, last commit 2023-10-01, stale.

tier_reason: Upgraded from B. The PVLDB 18(11) paper compares Sphinx with DHT, DHT-expandable, RSQF, Aleph Filter and Adaptive Aleph Filter, and names the CPUs (Xeon W7-2495X; 2x Xeon Silver 4314). The repo states the build: CMakeLists.txt gives -std=c++23 -O3 -march=native -mbmi2, and benchmark/reproducibility.md lists GCC 11.4.0. The public benchmark code (benchmark/benchmark_main.cpp, benchmark_tail.cpp and related files) runs all these baselines.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Abstract: about 2x lower query latency, update latency and memory footprint than the best alternatives. Fig. 6: zero false positives for queries to existing keys, and at most half the memory of the other baselines. In memory (Fig. 8), Sphinx has the lowest average and p99 query/update latency. Its average insertion is slightly slower than some baselines (read-before-write); Sphinx-4 (4 reserve bits) beats all baselines on every in-memory metric. On Optane, Sphinx variants are fastest. On SSD (Fig. 9), they match or beat all baselines, with only a slight gap to DHT-expandable under a uniform workload. Under skew at 90-99% cache hit rate, Sphinx is 10-35% faster than DHT-expandable (Fig. 10A).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: GCC 11.4.0 (benchmark/reproducibility.md, 'version installed or later'); -std=c++23 -O3 -march=native -mbmi2 (CMakeLists.txt). CMakeLists.txt also sets an RPATH to /usr/local/gcc-14.1.0 and has a commented-out GCC 14.1.0 compiler path.
corrections.stars_or_usage: 22 stars; PVLDB vol. 18(11), pp. 4424-4437 (2025); the paper's PVLDB Artifact Availability section points to the repo
corrections.caveats: The baselines are LSH-table indexes and filters (DHT, RSQF, Aleph Filter), not std::unordered_map or MPHFs such as BBHash, CMPH or PTHash. DHT is the authors' own C++ reimplementation, because the original is closed-source. RSQF and Aleph Filter come from the Memento Filter codebase. Sphinx is a dynamic succinct perfect hash table (a key-to-payload index), not a static MPHF. It is x86-only and needs BMI2 PDEP/PEXT. The 2x headline comes from the abstract; the figures carry the per-experiment detail and there is no numeric table. The compiler version comes from the repo's reproducibility doc, not the paper, and the CMake RPATH points to GCC 14.1.0, so the exact compiler for the paper runs is not certain.

notes: Upgraded to Tier A because the repo states the compiler and flags and the paper states the CPU models. I dropped the unverified 'ACM Artifacts Available badge' wording from stars_or_usage. The 'lowest latency everywhere' part of the claim was slightly overstated (average insertion, and the SSD case), so I narrowed it to what the paper says. Metadata matches gh: BSD-2-Clause, 22 stars, last commit 2025-08-31 (about 12.8 months ago, so stale).
